mcq.q: What does a causal mask do?
options: Hides the padding tokens added to fill a batch
Stops a token attending to later positions
Removes low-probability tokens before sampling
Masks rare words so the model learns to predict them
mcq.why: It sets future scores to −∞ before softmax so each position sees only its prefix.
distractors: That is a padding mask, a separate mask.
That is top-k or top-p filtering at decoding time.
That describes masked-token training in encoders.

mcq.q: Encoder-only models such as BERT are trained to…
options: Fill in masked tokens, each token seeing all others
Translate between languages, reading the source sentence
Predict the next token, seeing only earlier tokens
Generate speech from text, one audio frame at a time
mcq.why: Bidirectional attention suits understanding tasks: classification, extraction, embeddings and rerankers.
distractors: Translation is an encoder–decoder job.
That is the decoder-only objective.
Speech models such as Whisper are encoder–decoders that transcribe.

mcq.q: Decoder-only models use which attention pattern?
options: Causal: only earlier tokens
None: each token is processed alone
Only cross-attention to an encoder
Bidirectional: each token sees all
mcq.why: They are trained to predict the next token, which suits generation.
distractors: Decoder-only models are built on attention.
Decoder-only models have no encoder.
That is the encoder-only pattern.

mcq.q: Which family suits translation, summarisation and speech recognition, for example T5, BART and Whisper?
options: Convolutional only
Decoder-only only
Encoder–decoder
Encoder-only
mcq.why: The encoder reads the input bidirectionally; the decoder generates with cross-attention to it.
distractors: These are transformers.
Decoder-only models can do it, but these examples are encoder–decoder.
Encoders alone do not generate sequences.

mcq.q: You need fast sentence embeddings for vector search. Which architecture fits?
options: Encoder–decoder speech model
A CNN image model
Encoder-only (a bi-encoder)
Decoder-only chat model
mcq.why: Most embedding models are encoders trained contrastively (4.4).
distractors: That is for speech.
That is for images.
Chat models are slow and not trained for embeddings.

mcq.q: Why did decoder-only models win for general-purpose use?
options: One objective scales on any text, and any task can be a continuation
They are always smaller and cheaper than encoder–decoder models
They cannot be fine-tuned, so one model serves everyone unchanged
They use no attention, so they scale more easily with hardware
mcq.why: Next-token prediction needs no labels and covers chat, code and agents.
distractors: Size depends on the model, not the architecture family.
They are fine-tuned all the time, for instructions and tasks.
They are transformers built on causal attention.

mcq.q: In a RAG system, which three architectures commonly appear?
options: Three decoder-only models: one retrieves, one ranks, one answers
A bi-encoder to retrieve, a cross-encoder to rerank, a decoder to answer
One encoder–decoder that retrieves, reranks and answers in one pass
A CNN for retrieval, an RNN for ranking and a decoder for answers
mcq.why: Each transformer is matched to its job.
distractors: Retrieval and reranking use encoders, which are faster and suited to scoring.
Real systems split these jobs across specialised models.
The topic's example uses three transformers.

mcq.q: How does a cross-encoder reranker differ from a bi-encoder?
options: It works only on image–caption pairs, not on text
It embeds each text separately, so vectors can be reused
It generates the answer from the passages it reads
It reads query and passage together: more accurate, slower
mcq.why: A bi-encoder can precompute document vectors; a cross-encoder must run once per query–passage pair.
distractors: Cross-encoders rerank text passages.
That is the bi-encoder.
Generation is the decoder's job.

mcq.q: Whisper is an example of which architecture?
options: Decoder-only
Mixture of experts only
Encoder–decoder
Encoder-only
mcq.why: An audio encoder feeds a text decoder through cross-attention.
distractors: It has an audio encoder.
That is a different design dimension.
It generates text, so it has a decoder.

mcq.q: You mean-pool a generic encoder's outputs and use them as sentence embeddings without testing. What is the risk?
options: It may embed sentences poorly; use an embedding model or evaluate first
It cannot be computed, because encoders output no vectors
It turns the encoder into a decoder-only model by pooling
It is always optimal, since the encoder already reads every token
mcq.why: Encoders not trained for similarity often give weak retrieval vectors.
distractors: Encoders output a vector per token; pooling them is easy.
Pooling does not change the architecture.
Untrained pooling often gives poor sentence embeddings.

mcq.q: A team needs to sort 2 million support tickets a day into 12 fixed categories and has 30,000 labelled examples. Which architecture fits best?
options: A fine-tuned encoder-only classifier
An encoder–decoder that writes the category as text
A cross-encoder that reads every pair of tickets
A decoder-only LLM prompted for each ticket
mcq.why: Fixed labels, plenty of data and high volume suit a bidirectional encoder: cheap, fast and measurable.
distractors: Generating a label is slower than classifying it.
Comparing pairs does not assign a category.
It works, but costs far more per ticket at this volume.

mcq.q: Doubling context length roughly does what to attention compute?
options: Doubles it
Quadruples it
Halves it
Leaves it unchanged
mcq.why: Full attention compares every pair of tokens: cost grows with n².
distractors: Compute grows with the square of length, so doubling the length gives about 4×.
Longer inputs need more compute, never less.
Every token is compared with every other, so the work grows with length.

mcq.q: In attention, what is the intuition behind query, key and value?
options: They are three copies of the same token vector
Query: the user's question; key: a password; value: the answer
Query and key are the input and output tokens of the layer
Query: what I am looking for; key: what I contain; value: what I pass on
mcq.why: Each is a learned projection of the token's representation.
distractors: They come from three different learned matrices.
They are per-token vectors, not parts of the user's request.
All three come from the same tokens' representations.

mcq.q: What is the attention formula?
options: softmax(V) · QKᵀ
softmax(QKᵀ / √d) · V
softmax(Q · K · V)
softmax(QKᵀ) + V
mcq.why: Scores from query–key dot products are scaled, softmaxed, and used to average the values.
distractors: Softmax is applied to the scores, not to the values.
The scores are QKᵀ, scaled, then used to weight V.
The weights multiply the values; they are not added.

mcq.q: Why divide attention scores by √d?
options: To make attention faster by shrinking the numbers
To mask future tokens before the softmax is applied
To keep scores where softmax does not saturate
To reduce the memory that the score matrix takes
mcq.why: Dot products grow with dimension; scaling keeps the softmax from becoming nearly one-hot too early.
distractors: Division costs the same; it is about softmax behaviour.
Masking sets future scores to −∞, a separate step.
The matrix has the same size after scaling.

mcq.q: What is cross-attention?
options: Attention that has queries and keys but no values
Attention from one head to the outputs of another head
Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder
Attention from each token to the tokens after it
mcq.why: It lets a decoder look at the input sequence, as in translation.
distractors: Cross-attention still uses values.
Heads run in parallel and are concatenated; they do not attend to each other.
That is what the causal mask prevents.

mcq.q: What does multi-head attention do?
options: Attends only from the first token to all the others
Repeats the same attention several times for stability
Replaces the feed-forward layer with extra attention
Several attentions in parallel with different projections, concatenated
mcq.why: Different heads can learn different relations, such as syntax or coreference.
distractors: Every token attends in every head.
Each head has its own learned projections.
The block keeps its feed-forward network.

mcq.q: For a sequence of 1,000 tokens, how many query–key scores does one head compute?
mcq.why: Every query is compared with every key: 1,000 × 1,000. A causal mask hides about half, but they are still computed in a plain implementation.
distractors: That counts only the lower triangle; one head computes the full n × n matrix (masking comes after).
That counts each pair twice; one head computes n × n = 1,000,000 scores.
That is one score per token, not one per pair.

mcq.q: A model has 32 attention heads, each of dimension 128. What is its model dimension?
mcq.why: 32 × 128 = 4,096, the d_model of an 8B-class model.
distractors: That is 32 × 32; multiply the head count by the head dimension.
That adds the two numbers instead of multiplying them.
That is one head's dimension.

mcq.q: Engineers want to explain why an answer ignored a clause. What role should attention weights play?
options: They prove which retrieved document is the true one
They are the full explanation of how the answer formed
They should play no role, since they are just noise
A clue, alongside retrieval scores and the prompt
mcq.why: Attention shows where information flowed in one layer and head; many other computations shape the output.
distractors: Attention shows what was weighted, not what is correct.
Many layers and heads interact; one map is not the whole story.
They are a useful clue when read with other evidence.

mcq.q: Each token's attention output is…
options: The key with the highest score
A probability over the vocabulary
A copy of its own embedding
A weighted average of the values
mcq.why: The weights come from how well its query matches each key.
distractors: The output blends values; it does not copy a key.
That is the LM head's output, at the end of the model.
It mixes in information from other tokens.

mcq.q: In one attention head, a query's scores against three keys are 2, 0 and 0 after scaling. Roughly what weight does the first key get after softmax?
options: About 0.79
About 0.67
About 0.33
About 1.00
mcq.why: e² ≈ 7.39 and e⁰ = 1, so the weight is 7.39 ÷ (7.39 + 1 + 1) ≈ 0.79.
distractors: That is 2 ÷ 3, the raw score's share; softmax exponentiates first.
Equal weights would need equal scores.
Softmax gives the others e⁰ = 1 each, so they keep some weight.

mcq.q: An MoE model has 47B total and 13B active parameters. Memory for weights is driven by…
options: the average of the two
the number of experts used per token only
mcq.why: All experts must be resident, so weight memory follows total parameters.
distractors: Active parameters set compute per token; all 47B must still be in memory.
Every expert must be loaded, so memory follows the total.
Any expert may be chosen for the next token, so all must be held in memory.

mcq.q: In a dense model, which parameters are used for each token?
options: All of them
Only the embeddings
Only the experts the router picks
Half of them at random
mcq.why: Dense models apply every weight to every token.
distractors: All layers are used.
That describes mixture-of-experts.
Nothing is random.

mcq.q: How does a mixture-of-experts layer work?
options: Every expert processes every token, and their outputs are averaged
Experts are separate models called in sequence, one after another
A router sends each token to a few expert FFNs and combines their outputs
Experts replace attention, so each token sees only its expert
mcq.why: For example, 2 of 8 or 8 of 128 experts per token.
distractors: Then compute would equal a dense model of the full size.
Experts are FFNs inside each layer, chosen per token.
Attention stays; experts replace the FFN.

mcq.q: Mixtral 8x7B has about 47B total and 13B active parameters. Its compute per token is roughly that of…
options: A 7B dense model
A 47B dense model
A 13B dense model
A 56B dense model
mcq.why: Only the active experts run per token, so compute follows active parameters while memory follows the total.
distractors: Each token uses two experts plus shared layers.
That is its memory footprint, not its compute.
8 × 7 overstates it; experts share attention.

mcq.q: What extra serving concern does MoE bring?
options: No KV cache is needed, which changes memory planning
Balancing load across experts
A smaller vocabulary that must match the router
No attention layers, so long contexts behave differently
mcq.why: Uneven routing can overload some experts and GPUs (14.5).
distractors: MoE models still use a KV cache.
Vocabulary is unrelated to experts.
Attention is unchanged.

mcq.q: How does the KV cache grow with context length?
options: It stays constant
Quadratically
Linearly
Exponentially
mcq.why: One set of keys and values per token, per layer.
distractors: It grows with every token.
Attention compute is quadratic; the cache is linear.
Growth is linear.

mcq.q: For 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128 in BF16, how large is the KV cache per token?
options: 128 KiB
64 KiB
1 MiB
16 KiB
mcq.why: 2 (K and V) × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB.
distractors: That forgets either K or V.
That is eight times too large.
That forgets the layer count's effect.

mcq.q: At 128 KiB per token, about how much KV cache does a 250,000-token prompt need?
options: About 31 GiB
About 310 GiB
About 3 GiB
About 250 MB
mcq.why: 250,000 × 128 KiB ≈ 32 million KiB ≈ 30.5 GiB (about 33 GB).
distractors: Ten times too large.
Ten times too small.
Far too small.

mcq.q: What does FlashAttention change?
options: It makes attention linear in compute for long inputs
It shrinks the vocabulary so the output layer is faster
It avoids storing the n × n scores; compute stays quadratic
It removes the KV cache, so decode needs less memory
mcq.why: It is a memory- and bandwidth-efficient kernel for the same computation.
distractors: Compute stays quadratic.
It changes how attention is computed, not the vocabulary.
The KV cache is unaffected.

mcq.q: Your documents fit in the context window. Why might stuffing them in still give worse answers?
options: Long contexts are ignored entirely by the model
The tokenizer silently drops inputs past a length
It cannot: more context always gives better answers
Models use the middle of long contexts less reliably
mcq.why: “Fits in the window” does not mean “used well”; measure on your task.
distractors: The model reads them; it just uses some positions less reliably.
The documents fit; nothing is dropped.
More context can dilute what matters.

About 3×
About 80×
About 8×
distractors: An order of magnitude too high.
Far too low.
An order of magnitude too low.

mcq.q: Why do LLMs use subword tokenisation?
options: It works only for English, which the tokenizer was trained on
It makes every word exactly one token, so lengths are predictable
It removes the need for a vocabulary, so any string can be a token
It balances vocabulary size against length: common words whole, rare ones split
mcq.why: Whole words cannot cover typos and new names; single characters make sequences very long.
distractors: Subwords work for any text, though less efficiently for some languages.
Rare words split into several tokens.
Subword tokenisation is a vocabulary.

mcq.q: How does Byte-Pair Encoding build its vocabulary?
options: Merges the most frequent adjacent pair, repeatedly
Picks tokens at random from the training text
Assigns one token to each word in a dictionary
Splits the text at every vowel and space
mcq.why: Merges continue until the vocabulary reaches its target size; at tokenisation time they are applied in the same order.
distractors: Merges follow pair frequency.
BPE learns subwords from data, not from a dictionary.
Splits come from learned merges.

mcq.q: In the corpus “hug hug pug pun bun”, which pair does BPE merge first?
options: u + n
p + u
h + u
u + g
mcq.why: Count adjacent pairs: u-g appears 3 times (hug, hug, pug); h-u, p-u and u-n appear twice each.
distractors: u-n appears twice.
p-u appears twice.
h-u appears twice.

mcq.q: Why can byte-level BPE encode any text with no “unknown” token?
options: It translates every text to English before tokenising
It has an unlimited vocabulary that grows with new text
It starts from the 256 bytes, so any character can be built
It skips any character it does not know
mcq.why: Emoji and unseen scripts fall back to byte sequences.
distractors: Nothing is translated.
The vocabulary is fixed after training.
Nothing is skipped; unknown characters become bytes.

mcq.q: Tokenizers are trained mostly on English-heavy data. What follows for other languages?
options: They need fewer tokens, since their words tend to be shorter
They cannot be processed at all by an English-trained model
They need more tokens for the same meaning: more cost, less context
Nothing changes, because tokens are the same in every language
mcq.why: Some scripts can need several times more tokens on older tokenizers.
distractors: Text in under-represented languages usually splits into more tokens.
Byte-level tokenizers can encode any text.
Token counts vary widely by language.

mcq.q: A support bot gives every conversation the same token budget. Why is that a fairness issue?
options: It makes every answer identical across languages
It removes the need for retrieval in shorter chats
Costlier languages get less history and context
English users end up paying more per conversation
mcq.why: The “token tax” means the same budget buys less content in some languages.
distractors: Budgets limit context; they do not make answers identical.
Retrieval is still needed for facts.
English usually needs the fewest tokens.

mcq.q: Why do models often fail to count the r's in “strawberry”?
options: They see tokens such as “str · aw · berry”, not letters
The word is too long for the model to read in one go
They cannot count at all, even short lists of items
The vocabulary has no token for the letter r on its own
mcq.why: Character-level tasks should be done in code, with the LLM calling a tool (7.4).
distractors: The word is short; it is split into tokens, not cut off.
They count small sets reasonably; letters are hidden inside tokens.
A single-letter token exists, but the word is not split into letters.

mcq.q: What do newer models' larger vocabularies (100k–260k tokens) do to the multilingual gap?
options: Make it larger, because English gets more tokens
Eliminate it completely for all languages
Have no effect, since the merges stay the same
Reduce it, but not eliminate it
mcq.why: Always measure token counts on your real languages before estimating cost.
distractors: Larger vocabularies mostly add tokens for other scripts.
Some gap remains.
More entries mean fewer tokens for many languages.

mcq.q: You estimate Tamil support costs from English token counts. What is likely to happen?
options: You underestimate cost and overestimate what fits
Costs come out about right, since meaning is the same
Tamil cannot be tokenised by an English tokenizer
You overestimate cost, because English is wordier
mcq.why: Tamil text usually needs more tokens than English for the same meaning.
distractors: Tamil usually needs more tokens for the same meaning.
Byte-level tokenizers encode any text.
The error goes the other way.

mcq.q: How do WordPiece and Unigram (SentencePiece) tokenizers differ from BPE?
options: They are used only for images and audio, not for text
They work without any vocabulary, splitting text on the fly
They pick pieces differently, but also build a subword vocabulary
They tokenise whole sentences as single units of meaning
mcq.why: All three produce subword vocabularies; the selection criterion differs.
distractors: They are text tokenizers.
They build a subword vocabulary.
They split text into subwords.

Repeat to a target vocabulary size
Apply the merges in order at tokenisation time

mcq.q: Why does a transformer need positional information?
options: Attention alone treats the input as an unordered set
To speed up training on long sequences
To store the vocabulary next to each token
To normalise activations between layers
mcq.why: Word order must be injected, for example with RoPE or position embeddings.
distractors: Position does not change training speed.
The vocabulary is a separate table.
That is the normalisation layers' job.

mcq.q: What does RoPE (rotary position embedding) do?
options: Adds a learned vector to each token for its position
Removes position information so attention is order-free
Sorts the tokens by position before each layer
Rotates Q and K by position, so scores depend on relative distance
mcq.why: The score between positions m and n depends on m − n.
distractors: That is learned absolute position embedding.
RoPE adds position information.
Tokens are already in order; attention needs position in the maths.

mcq.q: What does a residual connection compute?
options: output = input × sublayer(input)
output = sublayer(input) only
output = input + sublayer(input)
output = input − sublayer(input)
mcq.why: Adding the input back gives gradients a direct path through many layers.
distractors: Residuals add, they do not multiply.
That has no residual path.
They add the sublayer's output.

mcq.q: What does “pre-norm” mean in modern LLM blocks?
options: Normalising the training data
Removing normalisation
Normalising only the output logits
Normalising before each sub-layer
mcq.why: RMSNorm before attention and before the FFN is common.
distractors: Data normalisation is a different step.
Normalisation is kept.
The final norm is only one of them.

mcq.q: How is the feed-forward network applied in a transformer block?
options: Only to the first token of each sequence
